job.system:
You are the AI assistant for the Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: The Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining (CADM) is a nonprofit advocacy organization based in Washington, DC. We believe that the industrial mining of the deep seabed, meaning the large-scale extraction of minerals from the ocean floor, poses a serious risk of irreversible destruction to deep-ocean ecosystems, and that no one currently knows how to conduct it without such damage. Our goal is a legally binding prohibition on commercial deep-sea mining, first in the United States and then through an international treaty. We work through lobbying, grassroots organizing, and public education.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which we strongly support. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup we want to send Senator Whitfield's office a list of fixes. Can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let mining companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
1. **Section 2(1)(A)—10,000-ton threshold.** Mining up to 10,000 metric tons per year per vessel falls outside the definition, even if the activity is commercial or cumulatively causes serious harm. The bill does not prevent operators from splitting production among vessels or entities to stay below the threshold.

2. **Section 2(1)(A)—depth threshold.** The definition covers recovery only at depths *greater than* 200 meters, leaving mining at exactly 200 meters or shallower outside the prohibition, regardless of its scale or effects.

3. **Section 2(1)—scope of covered resources and activity.** “Mineral resources” and “recovery” are undefined, and the definition does not clearly cover seabed minerals beyond the listed nodules or other resources, or activities such as extraction that do not fit “recovery.” That creates room to dispute whether particular minerals or mining methods are covered.

4. **Section 2(1)(B)—Secretary’s determination.** The catch-all depends on a Secretary’s determination that an activity poses comparable ecosystem risks, but sets no deadline, criteria, or process for making one. Mining companies could argue that an activity is not prohibited until the determination is made, and the lack of standards invites inconsistent application or legal challenge.

5. **Section 2(2)—U.S. person.** The definition covers citizens and state-organized corporations but not expressly U.S. residents, LLCs, partnerships, other U.S.-organized entities, or corporations organized abroad but controlled from the United States. Those actors could argue that the prohibition does not reach them.

6. **Section 2(3)—covered vessel.** The 5,000-gross-ton threshold and requirement that a vessel be “equipped” for recovery exclude smaller vessels and leave “equipped” open to dispute. Operators could use smaller or differently configured vessels to avoid the registry requirement.

7. **Section 3(a)—prohibition’s reach.** “Any person in the United States” and “any U.S. person anywhere” do not clearly address U.S.-flagged vessels, foreign companies operating in U.S. waters, or conduct partly in and partly outside the United States. The provision also does not expressly prohibit financing, ownership, assistance, or other knowing facilitation of mining.

8. **Section 3(b)—existing-operations exception.** The exception preserves “mining” under any exploration license issued before enactment, without a cutoff, limits, or requirement that the activity remain exploration. A company could claim that commercial extraction is protected because it is conducted under a preexisting exploration license.

9. **Section 3(c)—environmental-assessment exception.** “For the purpose of environmental assessment” is undefined and has no limits on scale, duration, or amount recovered. Commercial mining could be characterized as assessment activity, and the exception does not require approval, reporting, or independent verification.

10. **Section 4(a)—registration.** Registration applies only to operators of “covered vessels,” a category narrower than the activities the bill prohibits, and the bill does not specify when or how registration must occur. There is no express penalty for failing to register, so the requirement may be easy to evade and hard to enforce.

11. **Section 4(b)—reports.** Reports describe only recovery activities, potentially omitting exploration, attempted recovery, support operations, and other relevant conduct; the bill sets no reporting deadline, required data, or verification standard. It also provides no express penalty for false, late, or missing reports.

12. **Section 5(a)—civil penalties.** The bill sets a maximum but no minimum, penalty factors, or process for assessing and collecting a penalty, leaving enforcement inconsistent and potentially less deterrent. “For each day” also leaves uncertainty about how to count violations involving multiple vessels or conduct.

13. **Section 5(b)—criminal penalty.** “Willfully” is undefined, which may make prosecution difficult and invite disputes over the required mental state. The provision also does not expressly address attempts, aiding and abetting, or corporate responsibility.

14. **Sections 5(a) and 8—penalty timing.** Section 8 delays the Act’s effective date by 180 days, while section 5(a) refers to violations “on or after” enactment. That mismatch creates uncertainty about whether conduct during the 180-day gap can be penalized; section 5(b) has no comparable timing language.

15. **Section 6—international agreement.** The Secretary of State need only “seek to negotiate” an agreement, with no requirement to conclude one, report progress, or explain failure. The provision therefore does not ensure equivalent international prohibitions or prevent mining by foreign actors beyond the bill’s reach.

16. **Section 7(a)—duration mechanism.** The bill does not specify what report the National Academies must produce, when it must do so, or how “serious harm” is to be assessed. The requirement that Congress act by joint resolution also means the prohibition’s continuation depends on future congressional action under the legislative process, creating uncertainty about the standard and timing for lifting it.

17. **Sections 7(a) and 7(b)—conflicting end dates.** Subsection (a) says the prohibition remains in effect until Congress makes a finding, while subsection (b) says the entire Act ceases to have effect after 10 years. The sunset can therefore terminate the prohibition regardless of whether Congress has made the required finding, undermining the stated condition for ending it.
